summary: This standards-track memo defines a MIB module for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6 networks. Other MIB modules can extend it for specific tunnelling protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A tunnel carries traffic inside another protocol's packets. This document defines the SNMP objects a manager uses to see which tunnels a router has, what addresses they use and how they are protected, and to ask the router to create new ones.

questions: what is the ip tunnel mib
how to create a tunnel with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6, with one table to inspect them and one to create them.

tldr.problem: A router can hold tunnels of many kinds, such as GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TP and 6to4, and a manager needs one way to inspect them all and to ask for new ones to be set up.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the TUNNEL-MIB with two tables: a tunnel interface table indexed by ifIndex that describes the tunnels that exist, and a tunnel Inet config table indexed by endpoint addresses, encapsulation method and a manager-chosen ID, which can be used to create tunnels.
tldr.outcome: Tunnels of any type over IPv4 or IPv6 become visible and manageable through the same objects, with protocol-specific and security-specific details left to extension MIB modules. The document obsoletes RFC 2667.

facts.value: Address type, two addresses, encapsulation method and an ID

today: RFC 4087 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005. It obsoleted RFC 2667 and has not been obsoleted since. It remains the standard MIB for managing IP tunnels, with protocol-specific detail left to extension modules.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The IETF has specified a number of tunnelling protocols over the years, and this document describes a Management Information Base module for managing tunnels of any type over IPv4 and IPv6 networks. That list includes Generic Routing Encapsulation, IP-in-IP, Minimal Encapsulation, the Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol, the Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol, Layer 2 Forwarding, UDP tunnels, the Ascend Tunnel Management Protocol and IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels, among others.

Extension MIB modules may be designed for managing protocol-specific objects. Likewise, extension MIB modules may be designed for managing security-specific objects, such as those for IPsec, and traffic conditioner objects. The module does not support tunnels over non-IP networks; management of such tunnels may be supported by other MIB modules. The memo obsoletes RFC 2667.

For an overview of the documents that describe the Internet-Standard Management Framework, the RFC points at Section 7 of RFC 3410. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB, and MIB objects are generally accessed through SNMP. The module is compliant with SMIv2, described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: One set of objects covers every kind of tunnel over IP. Details that belong to a particular tunnelling protocol, or to a particular security protocol, are left to other MIB modules that can be added later.

sections.title: Two Current Tables and One Deprecated
sections.content:
The module contains two current tables and one deprecated table. The current tables are the Tunnel Interface Table, which holds information on the tunnels known to a router, and the Tunnel Inet Config Table, which can be used for dynamic creation of tunnels and also provides a mapping from endpoint addresses to the current interface index value.

The version of the module that appeared in RFC 2667 contained the Tunnel Config Table, which mapped IPv4 endpoint addresses to interface indexes. It is now deprecated in favour of the Tunnel Inet Config Table.

The use of two different tables was an important design decision. Traditionally, ifIndex values are chosen by agents and are permitted to change across restarts. Allowing row creation directly in the Tunnel Interface Table, which is indexed by ifIndex, would complicate row creation and cause interoperability problems, because each agent might have special restrictions on ifIndex. Instead, a separate table is used that is indexed only by objects over which the manager has control: the addresses of the tunnel endpoints and the encapsulation protocol. Finally, an additional manager-chosen ID is used in the index, to support protocols such as L2F which allow multiple tunnels between the same endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: One table describes tunnels that exist and is keyed by the interface number the router assigns. The other is keyed by the addresses and encapsulation the manager chooses, so the manager can create a tunnel by adding a row.

sections.title: Tunnels and the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
Each logical interface, physical or virtual, has an ifEntry in the Interfaces MIB, RFC 2863. Tunnels are handled by creating a logical interface for each tunnel. These are then correlated, using the ifStack table of the Interfaces MIB, to those interfaces on which the local IPv4 or IPv6 addresses of the tunnels are configured. The model is a set of tunnel interfaces, such as an IP-in-IP tunnel and a GRE tunnel, sitting above a physical interface, with the attachment to the underlying interfaces provided by the ifStack table.

The ifRcvAddressTable usage can be defined in the MIB modules defining the encapsulation below the network layer, and holds the local IP addresses on which decapsulation will occur. If IP-in-IP encapsulation is being used, for example, the ifRcvAddressTable can be defined by IP-in-IP. If it is not specified, the default is that one entry will exist for the tunnel interface, where ifRcvAddressAddress contains the local IP address used for encapsulation and decapsulation, that is, the tunnelIfLocalInetAddress in the Tunnel Interface Table. The ifEntry itself is defined in the MIB module defining the encapsulation below the network layer, so for IP-in-IP encapsulation the ifEntry is defined by IP-in-IP.

The ifType of a tunnel should be set to 'tunnel' (131), and an entry in the IP Tunnel MIB module exists for every ifEntry with this ifType. An implementation may allow ifEntries to be created via the tunnelConfigTable. Creating a tunnel adds an entry in the ifTable and in the tunnelIfTable, and deleting a tunnel deletes the entries in both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel appears as an interface of its own, stacked above the physical interface it runs over. The stack table in the Interfaces MIB records that relationship, and the interface type of a tunnel is the number 131.

sections.title: The Tunnel Interface Table
sections.content:
The tunnelIfTable holds one row per configured tunnel, indexed by ifIndex. Its objects describe the tunnel. tunnelIfEncapsMethod gives the encapsulation method used by the tunnel. tunnelIfHopLimit is the IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit to use in the outer IP header, where a value of 0 indicates that the value is copied from the payload's header. tunnelIfSecurity states the method used to secure the outer IP header, with values none, ipsec and other, where ipsec indicates that IPsec is used between the tunnel endpoints for authentication, encryption or both; more specific security information may be available in a MIB module for the security protocol in use.

tunnelIfTOS is the method used to set the high 6 bits, the Differentiated Services codepoint, of the IPv4 TOS or IPv6 Traffic Class in the outer IP header. A value of -1 indicates that the bits are copied from the payload's header, -2 indicates that a traffic conditioner is invoked and more information may be available in a traffic conditioner MIB module, and a value between 0 and 63 inclusive sets the field to that value. The RFC notes that a better name would have been tunnelIfDSCPMethod, but the existing name appeared in RFC 2667 and existing objects cannot be renamed. tunnelIfFlowLabel is the method used to set the IPv6 Flow Label, and need not be present in rows where the tunnel is not over IPv6.

The address objects are tunnelIfAddressType, which gives the type of address used, tunnelIfLocalInetAddress, the source address used in the outer IP header, and tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress, the destination address used in the outer IP header. If the local address is unknown the value is 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 or :: for IPv6. If the remote address is unknown, or the tunnel is not a point-to-point link such as a 6to4 tunnel, the same zero values are used. tunnelIfEncapsLimit is the maximum number of additional encapsulations permitted for packets undergoing encapsulation at this node, where -1 indicates no limit. The IPv4-only objects tunnelIfLocalAddress and tunnelIfRemoteAddress are deprecated in favour of the version-agnostic ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row says how the tunnel is built: the encapsulation used, the addresses at each end, the hop limit and traffic class to put in the outer header, and whether the outer header is protected.

sections.title: Creating Tunnels
sections.content:
The tunnelInetConfigTable is indexed by five objects over which the manager has control: tunnelInetConfigAddressType, tunnelInetConfigLocalAddress, tunnelInetConfigRemoteAddress, tunnelInetConfigEncapsMethod and tunnelInetConfigID. Its rows map a set of tunnel endpoints to the associated ifIndex value, and it can also be used for row creation. Every row in the tunnelIfTable with a fixed destination address should have a corresponding row in the tunnelInetConfigTable, regardless of whether it was created via SNMP.

The local address column carries 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 or :: for IPv6 if the device is free to choose any of its addresses at tunnel establishment time. tunnelInetConfigIfIndex holds the interface index of the tunnel, tunnelInetConfigStatus is the row status used to create and delete rows, and tunnelInetConfigStorageType says whether the row is permanent, read-only or not stored.

The RFC also warns about a limit. There is a 128 sub-identifier maximum for object identifiers. If the total number of octets in tunnelInetConfigLocalAddress and tunnelInetConfigRemoteAddress exceeds 110, the object identifiers of column instances in this table will have more than 128 sub-identifiers and cannot be accessed using SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3. In practice this is not expected to be a problem, since IPv4 and IPv6 addresses will not cause the limit to be reached, but if an agent supports other types, care must be taken that the sum of the lengths does not exceed the limit.
sections.plainLanguage: To ask for a new tunnel, the manager creates a row keyed by the two addresses, the encapsulation method and an ID it chooses. The router fills in the interface number. The address columns can be short, because the device may pick its own local address.

sections.title: The IANA Tunnel Type Convention
sections.content:
The document introduces a new IANA-maintained textual convention, IANAtunnelType, added to the IANAifType-MIB. The initial version of the convention is in Appendix A of the RFC, and the current version is published by IANA. The assignment policy for IANAtunnelType values should always be identical to the policy for assigning IANAifType values.

New types of tunnels over IPv4 or IPv6 should not be assigned IANAifType values. Instead they should be assigned IANAtunnelType values and hence reuse the interface type tunnel(131). That restriction does not apply to 'tunnels' which are not over IPv4 or IPv6. Previously, tunnel types that were not point-to-point tunnels were problematic, because they could not be properly expressed in the tunnel MIB, and hence were assigned IANAifType values. This document corrects that problem, and as a result IANA has deprecated the sixToFour(215) IANAifType value in favour of the sixToFour(11) IANAtunnelType value.
sections.plainLanguage: New kinds of tunnel get a number in a separate list rather than a new interface type, so that every tunnel can keep the same interface type, 131.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects in this module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. Unauthorized write access to any of the writable objects could cause unauthorized creation or manipulation of tunnels, resulting in a denial of service, or redirection of packets to an arbitrary destination.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP. Unauthorized read access to tunnelIfLocalInetAddress, tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress, tunnelIfLocalAddress, tunnelIfRemoteAddress, or any object in the tunnelConfigTable or tunnelInetConfigTable would reveal information about the tunnel topology.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects in this module. The RFC recommends that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is then the operator's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that access is given only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading the tunnel objects reveals the shape of the network, and writing them lets someone create tunnels or redirect traffic. The RFC therefore recommends SNMPv3 with its encryption and authentication switched on.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2667
sections.content:
The IPv4-specific objects were deprecated, including tunnelIfLocalAddress, tunnelIfRemoteAddress, the tunnelConfigTable and the tunnelMIBBasicGroup. In their place the RFC added IP version-agnostic objects that should be used instead, including tunnelIfAddressType, tunnelIfLocalInetAddress, tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress, the tunnelInetConfigTable and the tunnelIMIBInetGroup. The new tunnelIfLocalInetAddress and tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress objects are read-write rather than read-only.

The DESCRIPTION clauses of existing version-agnostic objects that contained IPv4-specific text were updated to cover IPv6 as well, tunnelIfFlowLabel was added for tunnels over IPv6, and the encapsulation method, previously an INTEGER type, is now an IANA-maintained textual convention.
sections.plainLanguage: The main change since the earlier version is that the objects now work for IPv6 as well as IPv4, with the IPv4-only columns kept but marked as deprecated.

items.title: Encapsulation

items.title: Hop limit
items.text: The IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit for the outer header. Zero copies it from the payload.

items.title: Security
items.text: How the outer header is protected: none, ipsec or other.

items.title: Traffic class
items.text: How the 6-bit codepoint of the outer header is set: copied from the payload, set to a value, or left to a traffic conditioner.

items.title: Addresses
items.text: The local and remote endpoints, with the type of address given separately.

items.title: Encapsulation limit
items.text: How many further encapsulations a packet may get at this node. Minus one means no limit.
